title: 3-Read Friday #36: Attention Contagion, Independent Learning, and Email Feedback
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #36 links research on peer attention, independent-learning strategy, and a debate on email feedback. Barton praises Andrew Watson's breakdown of 'attention contagion' research -- the finding that a neighbouring student's attentiveness can spread to others -- as one of his favourite papers Watson has covered. Alex Quigley offers concrete strategies for building independent learners, including a 'name it, then frame it' approach Barton particularly likes. Paul Cline responds to Tom Sherrington's argument that email feedback after lesson observations is largely ineffective; Barton sides with Sherrington but values Cline's pushback.
points: Barton calls the 'attention contagion' research Watson covers 'one of my favourite research papers,' praising Watson's habit of surfacing findings, classroom implications, and caveats together.
He highlights Quigley's 'name it, then frame it' approach to teaching independent-learning strategies as a standout practical takeaway.
He discloses his own position in the Sherrington-vs-Cline debate over email feedback -- 'I am on Tom's side' -- while still valuing Cline's counter-argument as worth reading.
quotes: I love how Andrew dissects interesting research studies, picks out the main findings, discusses the implications for the classroom, and draws attention to important caveats.
Here, he breaks down one of my favourite research papers on the phenomenon of attention contagion.
A roomful of independent learners is the holy grail for many teachers. But achieving it is far from easy.
Here, Alex suggests some concrete strategies that can help. I really like the 'name it, then frame it' approach.
For what it’s worth, I am on Tom’s side of the debate here, but it is always worth being challenged by alternative perspectives.
